title: A Simple Object
objective: Create an object literal and read its properties with dot and bracket notation.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; this book chapter covers both arrays and objects — Code Forge splits them into separate chapters. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: An object groups related values together under named keys, instead of positions like an array. You create one with curly braces: a set of key: value pairs separated by commas, like const recruit = { name: "Ada", rank: "apprentice" };.

Dot notation is the usual way to read a property: recruit.name gives you "Ada". Bracket notation does the same thing with a string instead: recruit["name"] — you need brackets when the key isn't known until the program runs, or isn't a valid identifier.
Reading a property that doesn't exist doesn't throw an error in JavaScript — it just gives you undefined, which is useful to know when you're debugging a typo in a property name.
explanation.rule: Read a property with obj.key or obj["key"] — a missing key gives undefined instead of an error.

examples.title: Creating and Reading an Object
examples.note: Dot notation and bracket notation both reach the same property.

examples.title: A Missing Property
examples.note: rank was never set on this object, so JavaScript gives back undefined instead of raising an error.

checks.question: const item = { label: "Sword" }; what does item.price evaluate to?

feedback.correct: Correct — a missing property reads as undefined, not an error.
feedback.incorrect: Reading a property that was never set doesn't throw in JavaScript — it gives undefined.

assignment.title: Smith Card
assignment.brief: Write smithCard(name, rank) that builds an object with keys name and rank set from the arguments, then logs the name followed by the rank on the next line.
requirements: Build an object with a name key and a rank key.
Log the name, then log the rank on the next line.

requirementChecks.label: Builds an object with a name key

hints: Build the object first: { name: name, rank: rank }.
You can store it in a variable, or build it inline — either works.
card.name reads the name property back out of the object.
Log name on one line, then rank on the next.
